newsitem.title: USA: Motorola Q2 operating earnings top estimates.
newsitem.headline: Motorola Q2 operating earnings top estimates.

text.p: Technology giant Motorola Inc. posted better-than-expected second-quarter operating results Tuesday -- evidence, analysts said, that a turnaround in the company's key industries is well under way.

Net income, however, was hurt by a $170 million charge for phasing out its struggling dynamic random access memory (DRAM) business, and the company said additional restructuring charges may be taken in the second half of the year.
After the market closed Tuesday, Schaumburg, Ill.-based Motorola reported second-quarter earnings of $268 million including the charge, compared with $326 million last year.
Earnings per share excluding the charge were 62 cents a share. The consensus analyst estimate was 56 cents a share, according to the First Call service.
Motorola said revenues rose 10 percent to $7.5 billion, also higher than the expected $7.0 billion to $7.15 billion.

"We were looking for some upside and they delivered," Cowen & Co. analyst Wojtek Uzdelewicz said. "Orders seem to be pointing in the right direction overall. ... This is strong evidence the company is turning around."
Motorola stock Tuesday hit $83, its highest level in about two years, before closing up $2.125 at $82.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Motorola said it is still reviewing its operations and redirecting resources to developmental programmes with the greatest potential.

"We have already taken actions as a result of that process, despite the negative impact of such charges on quarterly financial results. ... We will continue to position the company for sustainable long-term growth and profitability," said Motorola Chief Executive Christopher Galvin.
The company said each of its business segments reported increased second-quarter sales and orders.

Semiconductor Products orders rose 36 percent and sales were up 3 percent at $2.0 billion. Had it not been for the DRAM-related charge, the segment would have posted increased operating profits, Motorola said.
In the first quarter, profits were down compared with the prior year. The semiconductor industry as a whole had suffered a downturn, plagued with increased competition and overcapacity.

"It's a question of positioning and focusing on what's important," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst for investment bankers Gruntal & Co. "I think they cleaned up over the last few quarters and will look even better in the second half."

Cellular Products also posted a significant increase in orders, up 20 percent, while sales rose 6 percent to $2.8 billion. Operating profits were flat, however. Wireless phones have been hit with pricing pressure and stiff competition.
"Right now we're looking forward," Eraiba said of the division. "They're entering the second half with strong momentum."

Analysts said the lagger was the Messaging, Information and Media Segment, which includes pagers. It showed just a 1 percent increase in orders, and Motorola said the paging group in particular again posted significantly lower sales and orders from North American paging operators.
In addition, overall net margin on sales fell to 3.6 percent in the second quarter from 4.8 percent a year ago. The first-half net margin slid to 4.2 percent from 5.1 percent.
But overall, analysts said they were pleased with the company's optimistic outlook, and the possibility of additional charges later in the year was not surprising.
"They're going through every piece of the organisation with a fine-tooth comb," said Douglas Christopher, an analyst for Crowell, Weedon & Co.
